items.body: Cover photo and cover design by Cherim Built entirely from fragments from the Ored Recordings catalogue, Cherim’s Ğymaq reconfigures the label’s archival focus into something spectral and unstable by ways of heritage not preserved, but dissolved, stretched, and made to echo. Working with Circassian vocal traditions, shichepshin (violin), and pkhachich (percussion), Cherim constructs an ambient language where rhythm rarely settles morphing into drones and narrative gives way to atmosphere. The opening track “Batraz” makes this clear: voices hover refracted through reverb as if heard across distance or time. On “Ashemez,” chopped and pitch-shifted samples introduce a faint rhythmic insistence, though the emphasis remains on timbre—on how sound mutates, and lingers. What emerges is not a fusion of folk and electronics, but a dialogue between presence and absence. These are not “updates” of traditional material; they are residues. The voices of traditional singers Ramazan Daur & Kazbek Nagaroko read like an afterimage or as an aural impression persisting in the ear even after erasure, never immediately recognisable but always evocative relaying mostly on low pitch and bass frequencies. Elsewhere, Muhamed Batit, Zaur Nagoy, Gupsa Pashtova and others surface carrying with them the weight of Circassian history — particularly the unresolved trauma that Ored’s catalogue repeatedly returns to. In this sense, Gymaq aligns with hauntological practices: the past is neither revived nor resolved, but continues to press into the present as echo. Cherim’s detailed treatment of source material — stretching, pitching, converting to MIDI — never feels purely technical. Instead, it becomes a means of inhabiting memory. Tracks like “Hifitse” foreground texture, letting percussion and violin blur into something resembling underwater dub, while “Bgișhem” strips things back to a sparse, mountainous solitude with the faint trace of voices speaking of polyphonic counterpoint. The closing track “Jenibecre Habibere,” intrudes into The Caretaker territory playing like selected memories from a haunted ballroom with a sampled violin originating from Ored’s Bonfires and Stars Sessions, while offering glimpses of dream pop. Through this album, Cherim offers something ancestral: a space where rituals — Jegu, Mexsimafe — persist as distant vibrations. Gymaq is not nostalgic in any simple sense. It is a yearning for home that acknowledges its own distortion, a cry — true to its title — that arrives already filtered through time, distance, and loss. Cover photo: Tulip tree in the village of Golovinka, Lazarevsky District, Krasnodar Krai / Shapsugia. Photo by Lilit Matevosyan. Cover design: Milana Khalilova. Released on May 21st, the annual Circassian Day of Remembrance, Shyshagh: Imaginary Circassian Underground arrives as a subtle but significant departure from the concerns that animated much of Ored Recordings’ previous catalogue. If Cherim’s Ğymaq dwelt among echoes, spectral traces, and the unresolved weight of history, Shyshagh asks what comes after remembrance. Rather than focusing on trauma itself, the compilation presents a cross-section of artists using Circassian cultural material as a starting point for new forms of expression. The answer is deliberately eclectic. Maykop-born, Tbilisi-based Cherim moves away from the drone-hauntology and desolate ambient landscapes of Ğymaq, embracing instead a surprisingly intimate folk idiom. “Pari (Nothing)” and “Ut1ypsh (Let It Go)” are sparse indie-folk songs whose emotional directness recalls both Soviet-era singer-songwriters and the lo-fi melancholy of bands such as Low. The shift signals a different register of vulnerability. Temir’s contributions occupy another corner of this imagined scene. Built from archival Circassian recordings and fragments of Jrpjej rehearsal tapes, “Zechir” and “Duguj” transform ethnographic material into organic, skeletal compositions where field recordings, ghostly voices, and deconstructed electronic textures coexist. These are qafe — traditional Circassian dance music — without the dancing: music that retains fragile traces of communal memory while drifting into ethereal pop and ambient collage. The compilation’s most evocative moment arrives with Shkhafit’s “Ziguer (Something),” a collaboration between Timur Kodzoko and his son Astemir. The piece unfolds as a semi-improvised drone-folk meditation steeped into environmental sounds and centred on the shichepshin, the Circassian fiddle. It feels suspended between archaeology and speculation, evoking what the liner notes describe as “the ghosts of an unfulfilled future.” Nearby sits Zafaq’s “Chapshre Djegumre (We Heal and We Dance),” a raw black metal rehearsal recording rooted in Circassian melodic traditions while pointedly avoiding the clichés of folk metal. What makes Shyshagh compelling is not simply its stylistic diversity but its underlying proposition. Circassian culture is often discussed through the lens of preservation, loss, and historical trauma. Here, Ored imagines something else: a living underground scene stretching from Nalchik to Paris, Tbilisi, and Göttingen, one that draws on archives and memory not to reconstruct the past but to create new futures. As another May 21st passes under increasingly restrictive conditions, Shyshagh offers a quiet act of resistance — not through commemoration alone, but through artistic evolution. (Gianmarco Del Re)

Johnson), landing fresh on the ever-refined Poverty Electronics, a label that has quietly shaped its own groundbreaking corner of experimental electronics for well over a decade Like sunrise personified Apple Tree Brightness burns like sunrise personified as the latest release from datewithdeath (aka Travis D. Johnson), landing fresh on the ever-refined Poverty Electronics, a label that has quietly shaped its own groundbreaking corner of experimental electronics for well over a decade. Beautifully assembled across six pieces, the release opens with “Hir buttokez bay and brode,” a fourteen-minute drift through lilting fluid motion, gently plucked metallic repetition, and a softly looping detail that radiates warmth without ever losing its sense of mystery. Found sounds flicker constantly through the tender mix, giving the piece an almost tactile physicality. Track two, “(aar),” pivots sharply into fractured breaks and tangled sound sculpture, balancing distorted pressure against moments of apparently surprising tenderness within its compact two-minute runtime. There’s a raw physical charge to it, as though primordial rhythm systems are colliding with some half-corrupted archaic architecture.​ “tilde” follows as a slow-moving procession of clicks, chimes, and hovering drone. Its low mechanical hum recalls domestic ambience at its most strangely comforting, turning everyday sonic residue into something hypnotic and absorbing. “tttg-dyumed fS” captures the imagined strange excitement of early home-computing culture circa Sinclair ZX81 cassette loading aesthetics, moving with uncanny precision, all flickering resilient suspense and digitized anticipation, channeled through brittle electro-acoustic abstraction. By the time “XC” arrives, the release has fully surrendered to rhythmic elasticity: strobing pulses, clipped repetitions, and drifted proto-cellular pacing unfolding with installation-like intensity. Closing piece “(aee)” begins from a grounded resting tone before gradually unfolding into a landscape of industrial resonance and manipulated object sound, ending the album with a traversing and centered feeling of quiet swaying motion rather than mere resolution of a musical. Apple Tree Brightness is available on Poverty Electronics. [Bandcamp] Apple Tree Brightness by datewithdeath

items.body: Mutual Motion gathers 25 artists across 24 tracks into a release animated by movement, bodily response, and stylistic multiplicity—an expansive survey of modern club mechanics operating at full physiological intensity. Modern club mechanics operating at full physiological intensity Mutual Motion [BMR-V001] by Various Artists   Boston’s Body Method imprint returns with a compilation wired directly into the circulation systems of contemporary underground electronic music. Mutual Motion gathers 25 artists across 24 tracks into a release animated by movement, bodily response, and stylistic multiplicity—an expansive survey of modern club mechanics operating at full physiological intensity. The compilation refuses singularity. Breaks fracture and reassemble in volatile patterns, electro pulses with fluorescent precision, four-to-the-floor pressure drives forward with locked persistence, and techno structures scrape against the red line of physical abrasion. Drum & bass appears throughout not as retrospective gesture but as active propulsion—tightened, accelerated, and repurposed for present-tense function. Cinematic musical passages drift through the release like suspended memory traces before dissolving into unstable glitch architectures, while Djembe-derived rhythmic figures emerge from beneath the circuitry to introduce tactile human force into the synthetic framework. Organic percussion, hand-struck repetition, and tribal-inflected rhythmic motion create grounding points within the hypermodern landscape. The body remains the underlying framework: frequencies rise toward abstraction before descending back into low-end pressure, sweat, impact, and movement, each shift behaving like a separate organ in circulation. From f1 shifty’s club-focused opener through to DB Cooper’s rolling drum & bass lilt, Mutual Motion continually recalibrates its momentum without sacrificing coherence. Sohn Jamal & K Domestic inject elastic electro-funk mechanics, while Type 1 delivers a belting peak-time throwdown engineered for maximum dancefloor response. Roiju’s tribal-inflected organic rhythms bring earthbound tension into contrast with Brianna Paon’s sharply resolved production aesthetics and Ovid’s sophisticated command of arrangement and texture. Beyond these standouts, the wider Body Method crew maintain the compilation’s altitude with striking consistency. Nirborna, Talker, Raido, Miles Amillion, Libuse, Sel.6, Deroboter, and nxtel — whose contribution lands as one of the compilation’s outright killers—all submit finely tuned club constructions calibrated for movement and system pressure. Kala Btz, 619!, brvss/15ac, Arina Krondeva, Kruseros, Cades, Wiesma, Icky Reels, and closing artist Jagdabann further reinforce the release’s breadth, delivering tracks that balance DJ functionality with detailed production craft. Across its runtime, Mutual Motion sustains a recognisably high altitude, presenting Body Method as a label embedded within the current pulse of contemporary club music. Mutual Motion is available on Body Method. [Bandcamp] Mutual Motion [BMR-V001] by Various Artists

items.body: As a first collaboration of David and Scott, the feeling is immediately harmonically balanced and calming, the overall flow allows for sightseeing while you are napping. Cinematic tinkling satisfying hearts and minds, two chill guys, gentle souls making lovely music. Through The Thought Horizon is a melodic, beautiful, and deeply resonant album. Cinematic tinkling satisfying hearts and minds Through The Thought Horizon by David Helpling & Scott Reich   Celestial keyboards, electric guitar and piano, the feeling is slow with the reverb turned all the way up, past 11, or just completely breaking off the reverb knob. There are a lot of different Grand Pianos on this record. There is mystery without darkness. This album is about returning, not to what was, but to what is. What is home, what is who we really are. This music will not bring you there, but it might help you to consider that you are already there. The poet David Whyte once spoke about life being the place “where our need to express our own particularity is always in a conversation with life’s equally strong need to change us into something else.” Consider the conversational nature of reality. We innately know that we are here in this time and place in order to express something within us. Something important that can only come from us. Life cooperates by creating situations for us where we must express this, where there really is no other choice. Scott said that his creative process is his attempt to enter the inner sanctum, into the silence in which all music is born. That silence is like the original void from which all universes emanated. “This is a good analogue for David‘s studio. It has excellent sound isolation and it is dimly lit. Whenever I entered that place with David it was like a sacred space. This is where the lucent music spirits would visit.” Scott finds that the potential for good exists in all reality configurations. For this album David leaned heavily on his Yamaha electric grand (CP70) and effect pedals for much of the record. He also created some special electric guitar textures to support many of the tracks. His hardware instruments were recorded “wet” through a SSL analog mixing console including some of his favorite analog and digital synthesizers. There are a lot of different Grand Pianos on this record, all of them were sampled virtual instruments. Even still, Scott would improvise and record some of the piano parts when he was down in the studio. David reveals, “Scott is a gifted pianist and brings incredible modal changes and sophisticated chords… this makes this release unlike anything I have been involved with before. He comes from a jazz background, but is a deeply spiritual person… even more than that he is KIND, and that comes through in every note he plays. This record was a JOY to create and produce for me. Scott trusts me implicitly and I know exactly what he wants to say with the music. At the same time he has a very specific opinion about the music and can pinpoint exact changes or direction as soon as he hears what I have created or choices I have made. I LOVE this… this kind of open communication and love for a specific result made the production process very free and swift. Scott is very well read and is deeply steeped in poetry… specifically Rumi and Rilke. All of the titles for this record came from Scott’s world, including the title of the release itself. He would often send me the most beautiful quotes pertaining to our many discussions on consciousness, the divine and our place in this world and what may exist beyond it. Quotes and memes from these poets and contemporaries like Mooji kept me focused and inspired to bring these pieces together.” Sparkling sunshine in slow motion :: Opening with a single ping on the piano, the feeling is revelatory, with reverence and all that fantastic reverb, summoning forth oceans of calming waves,  “The Simplest of Miracles” (8:01) the piano tells the story with only sound. In the quiet part there is an orchestra, the dimensions expand and glow. An emerging piano melody with synth shadows follows, “Into Our First World” (4:55) the journey seems to drop off, reignited by piano tingles sending us over the edge and into the vastness of waking up in the morning. Quiet moments follow and gently flow together starting from light grey to full dense deep colors, “Source of the Longest River” (6:32) takes the listener flowing through very different territories in the same gentle slow pace, no hurries. Slowly, a piano emerges in a dream, gradual and careful, precise. We go into the void with all those colors and illusions, “Shadows, Stars and Dreams” (5:49) midway through the track there is a relaxing, the piano warms the way. Fading in, first as hints, followed by echoes, sparkling sunshine in slow motion, “Breath of a Flower” (6:14) brings in more instruments, electric guitar, chimes, electronics, suggesting the sound of flowers breathing gently in glorious microscopic detail. The next track might be a little bit sad, a slow piano, with illuminating washes, “Dream of the Last Morning” (4:40) brings hope, keyboards create magic. “Fallen Skies, Remember Me” (4:43) quietly emerges bringing a lyrical feeling, a sad love song, obviously with no words, just a melody that has a poetic meter, a tragic story of rising strings, it is heavenly. Starting from quiet the piano builds into a light funky jazz groove, “The Primordial Tower” (7:17) suggests a bridge to the sky, there is no darkness here. For the final track, the guitar rainbows wave slowly, “Through the Thought Horizon” (7:10). The piano comes up and upward we go, with pixie dust everywhere, sparkling and shifting. This whole album is like a finely crafted soporific, which is in high demand in times of constant stress. As a first collaboration of David and Scott, the feeling is immediately harmonically balanced and calming, the overall flow allows for sightseeing while you are napping. Cinematic tinkling satisfying hearts and minds, two chill guys, gentle souls making lovely music. Through The Thought Horizon is a melodic, beautiful, and deeply resonant album. Through The Thought Horizon is available on Spotted Peccary Music. [Bandcamp]

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Well, with a title like that, I just could not resist: Rodrigo Maccioni is certainly no fool and I am far from either blind, or deaf for that matter! Alejandro Vera handles the bassoon, Pascal Montenegro on English horn, Alfonso Vergara plays clarinets, Arianne Guerra the viola with bassist Eduardo Rubio and drummer Leonardo Saavedra, adding Jorge Bugue�o on electric piano and ably led by Rodrigo Maccioni on electric guitar, keyboards and flute. Now, to be fair, RIO/Avant is not necessarily within my expertise but If I am to be called a Prog Rogue, I must live up to being open-minded and occasionally swim against any tide. Also, I quite enjoyed Penguin Caf� Orchestra, so I should be okay. Vamos! The title track opens the curtains with courageous flair, a gigantic nearly 22-minute epic that takes boldness to new heights, an orchestral effect where all the musicians get to blend in and interface with precision. Overflowing with twists and turns and the occasional somersault, I was particularly captivated by the stunning viola and clarinet elements, as well as the muscular drum work and when the bassoon and horns kicked in, the amazement was palpable. Rodrigo certainly has a keen ability to marshal all the components into a cohesive centralized core, his mathematical electric guitar work showing not only rhythmic complexity, but the soloing can often bewilder with gushing emotional outcry. The arrangements are definitely intricately woven, the variations suggesting a hypnotic quality that cannot be ignored, and yet the entire opus is highly melodic and agreeable to the ear, with hints of dissonance and even playfulness that add the obligatory spice. Vergara's clarinet is often the highlight, as the warm sound of the instrument exudes a sense of fun that collides softly with all the surrounding mayhem. As far as experimental Prog is concerned, this piece is quite the mind-opener. The next three tracks are all under 8 minutes long and serve as sonic portals that seek to express various images that could have qualified as a suite, the reflective "Temple of Mirrors" aiming at more ambient scenarios, closer to modern classical soundtrack music. Here the strings are oblique, the percussion choosing percolation as well as propulsion, the bass boisterous and Rodrigo ripping hard on the fretboard. More of an experimental KC feel, Leonardo Saavedra channeling both his Muir and Bruford influences to perfection, a stunning slice of bravado. "When They Arrive" injects some mystery into the proceedings, the stark echoes of a science fiction scene apparent to these ears, somewhere between eerie and intriguing, the cacophony linear and purposeful, as the piano plays the conductor all along. The trilling sounds midway into the piece owe a sense of vibrating lizard tongues , amid the rhythmic aspic, a frightfully vivid touch that hit the mark. "Everything Stopped" explodes from the gates with furious abandon, shards of razor wire cutting into the skin and the mood bends into adrenalin-fueled numbness. The piano and English horn bounce off each other like two coy lovers, a synth painting the backdrop, the woodwinds curling delicately among the drumbeats, eventually led by the gripping viola into another sombre realm. Rodrigo takes over with a cyclical guitar pattern that settles the score into a more athletic environment. The insistence is punctuated by the bass /drum duo that shows little remorse in dragging the remaining instruments into the cauldron. A sustained final track ,"Memento Mori" summarizes the overall mood quite succinctly, a form of controlled bedlam that never seems to jar negatively, yet keeping the listener perpetually close to the edge, as if on a highwire. Peaks, valleys, entrances and exits are all undertaken to bring the listener to some distant space, a comfortable confusion that can never be predetermined. Kudos to all the musicians who weld together with apparent impunity, led by Rodrigo who never hogs the limelight, content to orchestrate the various engaging sounds and shaping them into a cohesive whole. This was quite the personal experience, especially for a fan of melody who generally shies away from dissonance and turmoil. It certainly helped with my blood circulation and overall cardiovascular disposition. A band I intend to follow. 4.5 Aconcaguas

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — WHALES DON'T FLY was formed in Bragan�a, Portugal in 2018 and is one of a slew of modern progressivemetal bands that dabbles in more than one stylistic approach attempting to craft a greater sum ofthe parts. This band features Rafael Alfonso on vocals and guitar, Jorge Rocha on guitar, Jos� PedroBoura on bass and Rui Pires on the drums. The band blends together various metal subgenres includingtraditional classic 80s heavy metal, groove metal, a smidge of sludge, thrash and even death metalout of the Gojira playbook however it's primary modus operandi is mixing melodic metalcore withprogressive rock structures.THE GOLDEN SEA is the band's debut and given it's emphasis on the progressive side crafts aconceptual narrative that tracks an ancient pilgrim's journey across a desolate landscape in thedesert that spans through nine tracks at nearly 56 minutes of playing time. The band's sound ischaracterized by heavy groovy guitar riffs with thumping bass lines, heavy percussion and shoutedlyrics in the metacore style all accompanied by lush dreamy atmospheres however it wouldn't be atrue prog metal album if it didn't also include moments of slowed down cleaner vocal-led passageswith cleaner guitars and a more labyrinthine song structure style.This band's debut is a nice blend of all the aforementioned elements and starts off promising with anice ambient atmospheric intro with "Ancient Mystery" followed by the first single "Man And ThePilgrim" which established the band's well-crafted style of subgenre juggling and all laid out inprogressive packaging. The production shines and the album is mixed quite professionally with a trueepic feel that prog metal is supposed to evoke. The newer releases from Gojira are very much clearinspirations but so are the harsh meets clean vocal approach of the Andorran band Persefone as wellas pretty much any melodic metalcore act like Trivium. The band promises a magnanimous journeythrough mystical lands but ultimately fails to exude such grandiosity with THE GOLDEN SEA.Overall it's a pleasant melodic ride on the more commercial end of prog metal with a been-there /done-that cookie cutter approach which serves as the primary problem for really finding this onecompelling as this style of prog metal seems played out and evokes the 2000s with an endless swarmof similarly minded acts having already tread upon these sacred lands. It's the type of album thatwon't offend but that's exactly where it falls short as it plays it all too safe hoping to be thenext hit on Spotify or something. While potential is looming in every nook and cranny on this one,unfortunately it seems that the band is loath to expand into meaningful terrain all the while tryingto impress with a multitude of metal styles thrown into the blender but yet resulting in a fairlygeneric display of ambition. It's good but honestly not something that beckons a return visit atleast for my liking.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Inspired by the amazing chemistry between of singers Anastasya Korol and Latifah Smith, San Diego's metal-grounded eclecticians have found a new direction: blending intricate multi-voiced vocal weaves over and within the boys' jazzified metal music.1. "Prelude" (1:32) an a cappella shanty performed as a layered four-part choral piece by Anastasya Korol and Latifah Smith. It definitely introduces the new approach the band is choosing for the album as well as sets the tone for the essential if not primary role that sophisticatedly-arranged vocals will have over the course of each of the next eight songs. (4.5/5) 2. "Pirates" (4:59) an amazingly fresh weave of near-liturgical choral vocal music with/within sophisticated heavy, metal, and Jazz-Rock Fusion music. The shocking first minute blows away, the vocal arrangements of the second impressing big time, while the jazzy instrumental third-through-fifth sucks you into its groove and keyboard magic while the finale reminds you that these sacred songs are sea shanties. A lot like INNER EAR BRIGADE! (9.25/10)3. "Gambler" (2:57) a very INNER EAR BRIGADE and iNFiNiEN-sounding tune with Anastasya and Latifah blending their voices over the funky prog music, sounding like something from SAY SHE SHE as well as the afore-mentioned quirk masters. Amazing! (9.5/10)4. "Ice Eater" (4:21) more incredibly refreshing sophisticated choral vocal weaving woven seamlessly within some awesome heavy jazzy prog. The vocal arrangements are so pert and professional, reminding me of so many of today's incredibly inventive female-led bands like A FORMAL HORSE, iNFiNiEN, INNER EAR BRIGADE, THE MOULETTES, PLANTOID, BILLIE BOTTLE'S TEMPLE OF SHIBBOLETH, RESONAXIS, and even HANDS OF THE HERON and LYNSEY WARD's projects. (9.333/10)5. "Archons" (2:33) the cheeky vocal performance here reminds me of both Aussie band RESONAXIS as well as KATHARINE BLAKE's projects and Billie Bottle's Temple of Shibboleth. Great theatric piano-based music beneath the vocal choir makes it all possible. Probably the most beautiful song on the album. Awesome! (9.667/10)6. "Desert" (4:23) Latin-infused heavy Jazz-Rock Fusion with a theatric weave of cabaret-like vocals intertwined within results in another tune that has a cheek and frivolity to it--until 1:37 when Matthew, Ryan, Nathan, and Kevin open a door to horror soundtrack music while Anastasya and Latifah provide the light wordless vocalese "ooh"s. Then the song moves through a few other syncopated motifs over which the vocal choir performs as if in ceremonial or theatric setting. Interesting and respectable but ultimately a little too jagged edged for me to maintain my engagement and/or enjoyment. (8.75/10)7. "Thing Eater" (5:48) another song based on even more dominating angular melody lines: presenting what feels like rock music that is much more constructed and composed around modern chromatic Classical Music traditions ("atonality," "Serialism," or "Expressionism"?). It's impressive but never as accessible or engaging as the album's other material. (8.75/10)8. "Elegy" (6:54) male voices in the choir! This piano-based piece feels as if it truly needs a house of worship for its presentation. During the first half of this I find myself reminded of 2000s Texas phenomenon POLYPHONIC SPREE while at others I find myself thinking of some of the great Broadway musicals I've heard (especially Stephen Schwartz' Godspell). Even the infrequent injections of aggressive angular electric guitar do little to detract from the celestial/liturgical or courtly feel of this wonderful piece of music. I think Katharine Blake (Medi�val B�bes), Hannah Moule (The Moulettes), Lynsey Ward and her Espera trio, and Bristol, England's Hands Of The Heron would be proud and envious of the achievement made here. (9.5/10)9. "Recapitulation" (1:16) a folk-feeling four-voiced a cappella vocal finale--much like the album's opener--to wind things up. A perfect ending to an incredible album. (4.375/5) Total Time 35:12I am so grateful for the drastically improved sound engineering and album length (the two criticisms I've posted for all of the band's previous three albums). I really love the way the band's vocalists have gelled--how they've become confident enough in the choral approach to their vocal deliveries. I don't know if Anastasya and Latifah are doing all of the choral tracks themselves (I don't hear male voices in some of the songs) but it's okay (brilliant!): whatever they're doing/however they're doing it, it's amazing! And mega-kudos to the guys for going along with, supporting, even whole-heartedly embracing it!A-/five stars; an amazing and totally refreshing album of progressive rock music, putting on display, once again, the fact that the new artists of the 21st Century have got all of the tools and brains to keep pushing the boundaries of possibility for our beloved genre of music.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — This Russian band's 17th studio album release! Can you believe they've been pumping them out since 2005! And, despite retaining a consistent core of musicians, they keep evolving.1. "Cendo" (5:54) electrified and effected acoustic guitar, fretless bass, gritty synth washes, and waves of cymbal sounds open this before the band launch into a jazz-rockin' motif that is rooted in traditional folk forms and melodies (amplified when Alexander Koryukovets' accordion joins in). The two concurrent lead guitar lines are the song's most distinguishing feature (aside from the accordion and Russian folk feel). Overall, I like it though it feels, compositionally, a little loose and unpolished to me (and the fact that Ivan Fedotov's drumming during song's second half feels out of sync with the rest of the band). At times it's just a bit too messy and cacophonous. (8.75/10)2. "Issero" (6:21) a very satisfying multi-motif song that starts out very warm and comforting--sounding like a blend of something from Robin Guthrie's chord bank and Paul Speer's atmospheric guitar world before Arkady Fedotov's antelope-like fretless bass enters with Alexander Kuzovlev's Steve Vai/Jeff Beck-like "floating" volume-pedal-manipulated lead electric guitar note play taking up the lead position. While at first I like Arkady's work very much, when he settles in the lowest registers of his sound capacity it muddies the song terribly--detracting from the rest of the weave. From there there are three other motifs, a brief bridge of synth-generated Ozrics/Kosmisches swirly sounds, a heavy fast-moving rocker over which Alex Kuz plays "mandoline" while rhythm guitarist Vladimir Ryabinin chugs along on some deep near-metal chords and then a final return (via folk instrument bridge) to Jazz-lite world music with gentle power chord strums of Vlad's electrified acoustic guitar and Alex Kuz's saz play. Overall I like this one pretty well. (9.125/10)3. "Joreil" (5:30) Alexander's use of saz as the lead instrument in this is welcome: creating a very inviting, very warm melody within the thick featherbed weave of heavily-distorted and -chorused gentle electric guitar strumming, driving bass and drums and, soon, accordion. Switching to volume-pedal controlled electric lead guitar, Alexander continues some excellent melodic soloing with Arkady Fedotov's acoustic guitar and Alexander Koryukovets' accordion also playing some nice "secondary" melody lines within the rich weave. A very pleasant, pleasing sometimes Greek folk-feeling song. (9/10)4. "Tio" (7:11) thought Alexander Kuzovlev's staccato lead guitar line provides the lead, I find Arkady Fedotov's bass play the most enjoyable and interesting thread of this song's first motif. In the early third minute the band switches into a new, smoother and more spacious motif as Ivan leads the way with brother Arkady providing the propellant for Alexander Kuzovlev's new approach to his Jeff Beck "Nadia"-like synthesized guitar lead. At the end of the fifth minute the band switches again onto a more forceful, Math Rock weave for a motif that has them traveling at a breakneck speed as Alexander shreds for a bit before settling into a mathematical melody pattern (even doubling it up with a second lead STEVE VAI-like electric guitar line) taking the song to its conclusion. Nice song! (13.5/15)5. "Akcani" (5:47) a song that is infused with a Russian folk feel not unlike Uzbekestan prog band FROM.UZ's earlier material. I like the use of unorthodox drum and percussion sounds as well as the doubling up of Alexander's main melody line by Arkady and, sometimes, Vladimir and Alexander Korykovets' accordion. The prominent use of the saz in the second half only solidifies the "Eastern" feelings oozing from this song (which I like). (8.875/10)6. "Plake" (6:53) the sound palette of this one has, for me, an almost-Caribbean flavor--like something one might have heard from world music artists Strunz & Farah or Govi back in the 80s or 90s but the hyper-speed pace provided by Ivan is much different than those artists, and then come the Kosmisches space synthesizer and mandoline sounds mixed into the weave. This is followed by another section with Alexander Kuz playing his volume-pedaled lead guitar followed by more straightforward axe playing for a bit before reverting to the "new" volume-pedal-controlled note playing. I like the world music feel of the first half but have to admit that this is one of those songs on which Ivan Fedotov's drumming just feels incongruous and unfit. (13.25/15)7. "Capitli" (4:30) a cool guitar weave, acoustic and electric, with great bass and accordion worked into the weave quite thickly while Ivan provides a wave-like rhythm track beneath it all. Alex Kuz enters in the middle with his lead electric, culminating in a bridge of staccato-chord pulses punctuation to transition us back into the gentler domain akin to the opening. Arkady's fretless lines here are great--matching perfectly Alex's volume-pedal-controled lead noteplay. I like this one very much. (9.125/10)8. "Far" (6:24) opening with more of Alex Kuzovlev's new Steve Vai/Jeff Beck-borrowed volume-pedal-controlled "centerless" note play, the band soon joins in providing another unusual world music (Caribbean/Yacht Rock) foundational weave for Alex to microtonally bend his notes over. The chorus "B" section finds the band traveling into some jazzier, almost heavy metal pathways while Alex continues his explorations of Steve Vai territory. The fourth minute is quite askew, feeling like a modern rock/metallized take on some of Dick Dale's 1960s Surfer Rock. Interesting! Never boring and, to be honest, not bad! (9/10)Total Time 48:30While I like the band's use of more regionally-traditional instruments (saz, mandoline, acoustic guitar, accordion) and the "world music" feels generated by such choices and combinations, I'm not as much of a fan of Alexander Kuzovlev's melody or sound choices. The Steve Vai/Jeff Beck like guitar tone/sound that he's now obsessed with is interesting but, in my opinion, is only a gimmick that should be used sparingly so that it doesn't get old or overwhelming, not on every song. As is not unusual, Ivan Fedotov's drumming, in my opinion, is occasionally unbefitting the music or weave: as if his sense of rhythm is different, even in conflict with, the rest of the band. The best and most consistently pleasing elements of this album's music, for me, are Arkady Fedotov's exquisite bass play and the enriching qualities of Alexander Koryukovets's accordion and Vladimir Ryabinin's comforting acoustic guitar tracks. Obviously, this album, for me, in no way reaches the heights of near-perfection that their 2023 masterpiece De ludo globi did. Still, this is another quite fine album: by no means a dud. B+/4.5 stars; another great collection of songs from these excellent musicians and unique craftsmen--once again defying categorization due to their idiosyncratic blending of diverse and eclectic styles and sounds. While not a masterpiece, this is not an album to be trifled with. Highly recommended.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Sleep Token made a name for themselves by fusing seemingly disparate genres like progressive metal,alternative pop and R&B on their previous studio album, which was an ambitious project that receivedboth accolades and criticism. Their latest studio album 'Even in Arcadia', the band's fourth, is noless impressive than its predecessor and definitely takes advantage of the creative impetus setforth by 'Take Me Back to Eden'. Released on the Sony-owned label RCA Records in 2025, this hour-long musical journey offers ten new tracks that display a streamlined, finely-engineered sound thathas thoroughly absorbed Sleep Token's alt-pop influences. 'Even in Arcadia' is quite easily the mostaccessible studio collection of theirs to date and is an album that impresses with pristineproduction and a variety of mainstream genres in the mix. The djent/metalcore elements are not asprevalent here, as they were on the band's previous studio project, which probably makes 'Even inArcadia' a tad bit more coherent and absorbing as an album, but also less dynamic and lessimpulsive.This record feels like a more personal statement for frontman Vessel, who is only joined by theband's drummer II, both of whom remain anonymous. It is interesting to see that Periphery's Adam'Nolly' Getgood has been involved with the production on 'Even in Arcadia' and given his work withother contemporary progressive metal bands, you can definitely hear that roaring sonic intensity inthe heavier sections. The opening track 'Look to Windward' is fabulous, and placing this particularsong in the very beginning draws you in and keeps you hooked for some time. Other key tracks include'Emergence', 'Caramel', and the 8-minute closer 'Infinite Baths', and while I am so much into thepoppier numbers, this album really has no weak tracks. 'Even in Arcadia' works pretty well on everylevel and is definitely going to be remembered as a solid entry in Sleep Token's catalogue.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 973Discipline is an internationally celebrated US progressive rock band from metro Detroit, adopting its name from the influential King Crimson's album with the same name. Discipline was formed in 1987 and during the early years, the leader of the band, Parmenter, augmented the band's live shows by changing into elaborate costumes for each song, inspired by Peter Gabriel's theatrics during his membership in Genesis. Parmenter's intensely personal lyrics, music style, as well as his ability to play multiple instruments, have invited critical comparisons to King Crimson, Van Der Graaf Generator, Genesis and Marillion. The band spend as much time working in Europe as they do in the U.S.A.The band's debut studio album "Chaos Out Of Order" which was released in 1988 as a cassette and was re-released in 2013 as "Chaos Out Of Order ? 25th Anniversary Reissue 1988 ? 2013", saw the group with Parmenter and guitarist Jon Preston Bouda, laying down the foundation of their very own sound that would be at their peak with their both studio albums of the 90's, their 1993 album "Push & Profit" and especially their 1997 album "Unfolded Like Staircase", which became probably their greatest masterpiece and one of the best progressive albums ever made. As "Chaos Out Of Order" was only produced on cassette format and was out of print for so many years, "Push & Profit" is usually considered the debut studio album by the band. These two albums reached to Discipline an international audience.So, "Chaos Out Of Order" is the real debut studio album of Discipline. The line up on "Chaos Out Of Order" is Matthew Parmenter (vocals, keyboards, guitars, bass guitars, violin and electronic drums), Jon Preston Bouda (guitars) and Woody Saunders (drums).I'm sure that few prog rock fans who were drawn to Discipline were aware that the album officially considered their debut, "Push & Profit", wasn't, in fact, their first full-length effort. Their real debut, "Chaos Out Of Order", is a raw concept album that blends early neo-prog with dark, classical and post-punk influences, capturing the band's nascent sound. In reality, "Chaos Out Of Order" is the only official concept album recorded by the band till now. It functions as an experience of "organized chaos", where the band explores diverse musical influences and textures. The nine tracks frequently connect to each other (follow), reinforcing the idea of ​​a real continuous and cohesive work that should be listened to from beginning to end to capture its full meaning. The lyrics are intense and personal, and deal with themes such as human transition, sensory perception, and states of consciousness. The album evokes feelings of isolation and desolation, but without falling into total despair, guiding the listener on a journey through the individual's "inner world".Some potential listeners will be put off by the material on the album falls far short of professional production standards in terms of sound. Nevertheless, those who accept the original raw form of the album will be treated to a rather compelling glimpse into the early days of Discipline. It's noted for its ambitious, long tracks featuring violin, saxophone and piano, reflecting a darker symphonic style that at times reminds me of Gentle Giant. Musically, it shows a band in an experimental phase, mixing prog rock with nuances of art rock and darker passages that would define their style.In "Chaos Out Of Order", the artistic quality of the material is astonishing. On one hand, the set includes completely youthful, naive musical attempts, while on the other, compositions not only noteworthy but also directly demonstrating that Discipline's melodic awareness, familiar from later releases, could be substantial from the outset, far from clich�, and yielding impressive results. This initial trio showcases Parmenter's great vocals and, while still unfinished, features polyrhythmic and complex arrangements, revealing the theatrical and dramatic musicality that would later emerge. From the two-part suite "Man & The Locust" to unexpected acoustic elements and a simple sound characteristic of North American music, this is a great work that captures the charm of their earliest period, which can only be found on this album. Interestingly, the tracks that eschew from the most progressive conventions fare very well, such as "Still Night", "Uphill Climb" and "Mickey Mouse Man". The previously unreleased 1987 track "Peacemaker" is included too.Conclusion: It's hard to imagine that "Chaos Out Of Order" would appeal to audiences outside the strict circle of Discipline fans. However, I really think that it was good that it's seen the light of day. After all, it's not only a missing publishing link in the objective perspective of the American's entire great career, but also the source of several truly successful titles that, even with twenty-five years, still sound like the "real" and fascinating Discipline. I also really think that "Chaos Out Of Order" is still a fascinating milestone in Discipline's history, as it represents the band's roots before they reached the amazing symphonic maturity of the 90's. Although the production is more raw than on later albums, it already reveals Matthew Parmenter's talent in songwriting and dramatic vocals. This is an album not to be missed.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by alainPP — "Cendo" stands out for its thunderous, Balkan-tinged folk-space sound, amplified by Alexander's accordion?a true virtuoso, it must be said; an easy-listening tune that invites daydreaming. "Issero" is ambient psychedelic from the outset; a track notable for the 'battle' between Alexander and Vladimir on their bewitching guitars over a cosmic flash. A heavy riff and the frenetic musical fire with the accordion induce a trance-like state, the mandolin not on MINIMUM VITAL but on a certain Greek island devoted to excess. Excess of notes scattered at will, imprinting a fresh new sound."Joreil" stands out for its acoustic guitar, its oriental folk atmosphere more than psychedelic. The gradual build-up with the accordion, the centerpiece of the tracks, before the jazz-rock guitar finale that levitates between two spheres, an innovative, melancholic, spacey outro. "Tio," for the vibrant guitar, I'll let the musician explain the technique; the atmosphere it creates leads us down a cloudy path, like raindrops gathering before falling. A moment of respite with the fruity guitar; I think of all those jazz-rock aces of the 70s who dared to unleash solos almost juicier and heavier than the guitar heroes; I think of John McLaughlin, Frank Gambale, and Al Di Meola. The finale with the musical rain now falling."Akkani" for a spacey bossa nova, a crescendo of sound from which the guitar carves its way across the stars. The accordion makes the piece warm, contemplative, radiant behind the folk guitar, the Balkans with this medieval setting suggested by the mandolin. "Plake" follows, same style, spacey sounds embellished with traditional instruments evoking the pacifist Great East. The wah-wah pedal is used to great effect, creating a hazy atmosphere for a while before plunging into a heavy, stressful, then frenetic sound."Capitli" shifts gears, a jazzy, barroom vibe with the sticky accordion clinging to the fleeting sound. The rich, viscous guitar hypnotizes the ear before the insidious break gently descends into melancholic turmoil. "Far" closes this unique album with an acoustic-electric duet of guitars gently juxtaposing, then frantically. Ivan on drums unleashes an explosion of the senses before giving way to the velvety guitars.VESPERO mixes everything together, adding a few spacey, psychedelic keyboards, and you have a fresh album to enjoy without moderation, far removed from the usual progressive conventions.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The stars aligned when Supersister recorded their second album; even the aura of their Focus bandmates was present, the ancestral European past alongside avant-garde modernity and free jazz. To the Highest Bidder demonstrated compositional growth, the same compositional rebelliousness, the feeling of transcending genres, but in a different category. A Girl Named You sounds with that same compositional freedom reminiscent of Frank Zappa's 1969 improvisations, and even Eric Dolphy.Taking the time to let the notes float...like leaves on the sea that the wind gathers...and with the freshness of early Jethro Tull, the darkness of late Doors...the sophistication of Jacques Loussier playing Bach in a jazz key...plus the wisdom of the very end of Pawn Hearts by Van Der Graaf Generator.No Tree Will Grow (On Too High a Mountain) begins like those Gong mantras...but a melody sung with such sensitivity that it transcends genre, making it immortal. And in that contrast of warmth and coldness...of wide and intimate spaces, Supersister finds its place, the right note, its star in the firmament.From grandiose arrangements to thin, minimalist notes, with barely any percussion, stripped down like a winter city in Energy (Out of Future). When the otherworldly keyboard and the already prominent drums draw us into a vast courtyard, revealing it piece by piece until we reach the upper floor and gain a comprehensive, all-encompassing vision, exemplified by the music when the organ joins in, bringing light and air.Robert Jan Stips' keyboards alone can convey the essence of Canterbury without needing to travel to Great Britain, because they reside in the mind and heart.With great skill, they could abandon classical arrangements... only to let them fall to the ground and then raise them up in a psychedelic way, mutating and playing along until they arrived at Higher, once again flirting with Bossa Nova and that sweetness of the 60s, the flute, and melodies that, unknowingly, would influence alternative bands of the early 2000s like The Beta Band.The most peripheral of the Canterbury bandmates would be one of the most psychedelically jazzy, without losing the harmony... always ahead of the curve in terms of technology.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — With an aesthetic reminiscent of A Clockwork Orange, it could be nothing other than the Canterbury scene transported to the Netherlands.That peaceful opening with the flute is interrupted by distinctly progressive tracks, which set them apart from pioneers like Soft Machine. Led by keyboards and heavily influenced by jazz, like Frank Zappa in his Hot Rats era.But it was more than just a collection of influences... there was something aggressive about this quartet, something unsettling. The piano possessed the modernity of the 60s masters, while the fuzz bass and drums, along with Robert Jan Stips' atonal vocals, imbued it with an unmistakable 70s aura.Memories Are New introduces a keyboard that distorts to the very edge of psychedelia, and since Marco Vrolijk was a drummer who mastered both the subtlety of jazz and the ethereal spirituality of Bossa Nova, he could perfectly complement these rhythmic shifts. 11/8 is unmistakably Soft Machine, and the keyboard's oscillations vibrate and mutate like a lamp whose energy is intermittent, illuminating at times and plunging everything into complete darkness at others. An electric guitar wasn't necessary when the distortion could come from the keyboard and the contrasts were layered with such audacity and speed. That's why it's an album that surprises, that takes you by surprise, subversive in many ways, just like the decade that saw its birth.At times they created cinematic atmospheres, as in "Dreaming Wheelwhile"... to denser offerings like "Mexico," with its oriental influences, accompanied by percussion, and an esoteric, almost revelatory haze... within reach... but evaporating like fog when the sun rises in the morning.A classic vocal section accompanied by keyboards, which then accelerates, introduces us to "Metamorphosis," a garage rock track with punk and acid krautrock influences... mechanically repetitive. "Dona Nobis Pacem" is like the calm after committing the crime...and new promises for the next chapter, which will not bring more of the same but new things from the same quartet.

items.album: LOST WORLD BAND A Moment of Peace (Crossover Prog, 2024)
items.excerpt: Review by kev rowland — Can it really be more than 25 years since Lost World released their debut 'Trajectories'? items.body: Review by kev rowland — Can it really be more than 25 years since Lost World released their debut 'Trajectories'? I raved over them (I think it is the only time I have heard a prog band where three of the players were from the Moscow Conservatory) and since then I have kept in touch with Andy Didorenko (acoustic & electric guitars, bass, violins, percussion, keyboard, backing vocals), although it was only after he asked me to review the recent reissues that we realised I had not heard their 2024 album which is why I am playing it now. For the majority of their career LWB have been a band, but this is better regarded as a solo project as while there are three drummers on different tracks, the only other musicians are Yulia Musayelyan (flute on one) and singer Phoebe Carter who is on three. In January 2022 Andy was full of creative energy and by the end of the month he had recorded four demos, but then Russia invaded Ukraine and nothing seemed to matter anymore. Fast forward a year and Andy remembered an anti-war song he had written with Vassilli some 30 years earlier, and resurrected this and another from the same period, provided different lyrics and the album started coming together.Right from the beginning of "Overture 2024" one knows this is going to be something different as the chaotic and over the top piano, bass and violins drive us headlong into "Crumble Down" and it is already obvious that this is not an album where Andy wants us to relax, but rather it is full of jagged edges so we are careful where we step. This is his musical reaction to what was taking place in Ukraine, ensuring that the listener knows it is intended not to be comfortable, and in many ways feels much like a modern classical piece of work than something which is obviously progressive rock. It is dynamic, full of contrast, and even the vocals provide contrast in that they are highly melodic when they appear, very different to the staccato elements, and with a multi-instrumentalist as happy on piano, guitar or violin, one also never knows what melodic lead is going to be next.Even the cover photograph is symbolic, as it was taken on Governors Island, which used to be a 172-acre military base but is now a public park. If only we could turn all military bases back to public land the world would be a much better place, but musically this album knows that is never going to be the case so instead keeps driving us along and making us uncomfortable. This is yet another great album from Andy, I wonder what he is going to come up with next?

items.body: Review by kev rowland — I have been a fan of Kristoffer Gildenl�w since the very early days of Pain of Salvation, since when he has undertaken an interesting musical career, working as a session musician as well as releasing solo albums, with this being his sixth. One of the joys of his albums is that one never knows quite what area he is going to explore and I was surprised to find him going back to his prog metal roots, throwing in elements of djent, mathcore, doom and more while always maintaining the progressive and commercial overtones which make him stand out. It is certainly a very different beast indeed to his last two releases, 'Let Me Be A Ghost' (2021) and 'Empty' (2024), and a welcome diversion.He of course provides most of the instruments himself but has wisely brought in a real drummer in Leo Margarit (Pain of Salvation, For All We Know) while two guests get a guitar solo each, Daniel Magdič (Prehistorical Animals, ex-Pain of Salvation), and Dutch guitarist Thijmen van der Meer. Somehow, Gildenl�w has managed to retain the huge soundscapes and emotions we expect from him, but has focussed much more strongly on the guitar, using different techniques and time signatures to ensure we never have too much time to rest and instead are always looking to hear what comes next and what is around the corner. Just when we think we have it all worked out he changes gear and switches to a different direction, going quiet when it seems we are heading to a climax, and then riffing hard when it appears to be heading to calm.The result is a thoroughly enjoyable and modern progressive rock album which touches on many different subgenres and is all the better for it.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — I was a huge fan of the Italian prog band's last release, 2023's 'Strings From The Edge of Sound', and this is by the same quartet of Valerio Sgargi (lead vocals, keyboards, guitars), Alex Massari (guitars), Alessandro Cefal� (bass) and Daniele Giovannoni (drums, backing vocals, keyboards) plus a few guests including Adam Holzman and Randy McStine. This release is a concept, exploring the idea of a relationship between human and humanoid, and what exactly that means. It may feel like science fiction to some but given the advancements in AI there may well be a point in the future when AI stops guessing (current state) and does become sentient (future, although some may feel it is already here).I have reviewed all of Karmamoi's releases to date, apart from the 2011 debut and the remixed version of their last one, and my main issue with them is their inconsistency (at least to my ears), and while I firmly believe their last album was probably their finest, this sees a step in the wrong direction. The reason for that is that while the arrangements and performances are very polished and emotional, it also comes across as being all on the same level with little real depth. Given the topic being covered one would expect dynamic swings and changes but there is simply not enough real contrast so instead of coming across as being highly dramatic it all seems a little bland.When they do move in a different direction, such as on "The Mirror", it feels very much out of place with the rest of the album and all of a sudden, I get the impression I am in a theatre and there is a spotlight on the lead singer who is emoting to us all. In the end it all feels a little too much and I am somewhat drained by the end and not enjoying the experience. I am sure there are some who will feel this is of the very highest order, but this one is not for me.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — This is not the first time that Jordsj� and Breidablik have released an album together, as back in 2016 there was 'Songs From The Northern Wasteland', but that featured multiple songs from each band. This time around each band has a side to themselves for just one long piece, in each case titled "Kontraster". The other main difference between the two albums is that when the first was released, Breidablik was very much a solo project from keyboard player Morten Birkeland Nielsen, but in recent years he brought in firstly Hakon Oftung (guitar, flute) from Jordsj� to play on 2020's 'Omicron', and then drummer Trond Gjellum to also play on 2022's 'Alduorka' so it is this trio on Side B while Hakon also provides keyboards and vocals on Side A and is of course joined by drummer Kristian Frland. It was only recently that I raved over Jordsj�'s latest release, 'Pestkr�nikene', and yet again I find I am taken back in time to the heyday of commercial progressive rock and the early to mid-Seventies. It is relaxed, inviting, and again feels very analogue and one is never sure if we are going to spend more time in the realms of folk or symphonic, and while some could argue that it is all about Oftung and his skills as a multi-instrumentalist, the playing of Frland takes it to a whole new level and there are times when he remind me of Bill Bruford, at others Neal Peart. At 20 minutes in length I think this is the longest track recorded by the duo, and it will be interesting to see if they repeat the experiment as this if fascinating throughout and never overstays its welcome as it is comprised of so many individual sections.Even though Oftung plays on both sides, his role under Nielsen is very different indeed, as one would expect from working with an electronics wizard who has long been influenced by Tangerine Dream and for whom working on lengthy pieces is nothing new. Although I enjoy electronic music as much as the next proghead, for some reason I had not come across Breidablik prior to this joint release, but now I have I can see I am going to have to investigate further as this is highly polished and dramatic. Again, this never feels as if it is something modern but feels as if it is coming to us from the end of the Seventies when electronic bands were starting to make their presence felt and one can certainly imagine this forming part of a film soundtrack, especially if we were following reindeer in the snow across mountains and valleys. At least that is what I "see" while listening to this.Overall this is a great introduction to both bands and highly recommended for progheads who wish the last 50 years had not taken place.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Here is the latest release from one of my favourite improvisational acts, �resund Space Collective, which this time around is a split album with Hungarian outfit Psychedelic Source Records who cite �SC as being one of their major influences. Side A is one long jam, "Zephyr In Orbit" and rarely feels improvised as �SC feel incredibly tight on this with Mattias and Jiri keeping the foundation soundly locked down, keyboard players Love and Dr. Space knowing when to provide background and when to drift to the fore and Jonathan often allowing his guitar to be strident and in your face. This must be one of the most connected pieces I have come across from these guys, and even though it is more than 21 minutes long it never feels as if it has overstayed its welcome and, in many ways, acts as a great introduction to the band if a listener has wondered where to start.Psychedelic Source Records is a new name to me, and it is obviously they are highly influenced by �SC but in some ways they are even more of a collective in that over the course of the three tracks no musician plays on more than two, and many play on just one, so over the two quartets and one trio featured over the three songs on Side B there are 9 different musicians, with no-one playing on more than one song with any other musician. One might think this would mean incredibly varied music, but the result never sounds as if it comes from different bands, as they have their spaced-out psychedelia firmly front of mind at all times. I know that if I had more time, I would investigate their catalogue as it is currently possible to purchase all 101 of their releases from Bandcamp for a total price of just ?1 or more, but I'll never get any more reviewing done if I succumb to that temptation.As it is, this release is a great introduction to two highly imaginative improvisational outfits, and is definitely worthy of investigation.

items.body: There has already been considerable buzz surrounding the Norwegian artist Tazer, who, after a string of remarkable singles, is now unleashing the debut album, “Taze Is The Rule”. From the very first seconds, the album grabs you by the throat, firing relentless dark Electro sequences and pounding beats straight at the listener. Occasional guitar riffs are thrown into the mix as if even more power were needed. Industrial, Techno, and EBM collide in a fierce hybrid sound that bursts from the speakers at maximum intensity. Add possessed, aggressive vocal lines to the equation, and you begin to understand what Tazer is all about. There is not a single moment of respite across the album. Track after track hits with unrelenting force, as if a sonic atomic war has been declared and there is no escape from the fallout. Tazer sounds hard, aggressive, and uncompromising, yet at the same time feels like an absolute revelation—a project brimming with immense potential. One thing is certain: this is only the beginning, and you will undoubtedly be hearing much more from Tazer in the future. You can either seek shelter in a nuclear bunker or simply surrender to the project’s brutal yet irresistibly infectious assault. “Taze Is The Rule” leaves little room for anything in between. (Rating:9). Listen to “Taze Is The Rule”: https://hellektrokution.bandcamp.com/track/taze-is-the-rule

items.body: With the German band Days Of Sorrow, we dive back into the magic of the 1980s. The band was already active during that decade before disappearing a few years later. Yet some bands never truly vanish; they continue to linger in the collective memory of the fans, waiting for the right moment to come back to life. Apparently, the musical spark had never completely faded within the band itself either, because now they are back. Founded in Germany in 1981 by William Lennox and André Schreiber, Days Of Sorrow gained recognition through their melancholic, synth-driven songs, immortalized on releases such as “Remembering The Days” (1984) and “Wild World” (1986). More than three decades later, the band returned with renewed energy and a clear artistic vision. Since their reunion in 2018, Days Of Sorrow has proven to be far more than a nostalgic revival. With the album “Soulmate Sister”, the EP “No Fear”, and numerous live performances, the group has steadily built a compelling second chapter in its career. This year, that chapter was further strengthened with the release of “Raptures” available via Mots Music. “Raptures” is a brilliant opus in which Synth-Pop, enriched with subtle EBM elements, unfolds across ten outstanding tracks. Personally, I consider it one of the finest releases I have heard in recent years within the broad spectrum of Electro-Pop. I had the pleasure of speaking with William Lennox about the band’s past, present, and the creative journey that led to this remarkable new album. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: The origins of Days Of Sorrow date back to the very beginning of the 1980s, but the project came to an abrupt halt nearly 40 years ago, only to be revived a few years ago. How do you look back on the young musicians you were back then and on what you achieved at the time? And how did the reset or restart with the current lineup come about? William: Back then we were hungry for the music we loved and given the opportunities with affordable synths and drum machines we enjoyed experimenting all aspects. The result was a reflection of our state of mind, feeling and the environment we lived in, with Dortmund being a very industrial area back then. We didn´t particular look on any achievement rather than the excitement and new experiences of getting the chance to produce music, making a record and playing live. After all this time Andrè (bass and keys) and myself met again. Talking about music and the time in the 80´s, we soon found out that we were still in love with this kind of music and atmosphere it represents. But we didn´t just wanted to replicate this but take it further, meaning writing new songs, making new records. We took Frank (keys) on board, an old friend and producer from that time and recorded “Soulmate Sister”. Unfortunately, André had to quit out for personal reasons and we then asked Kati and Jojo to join us with their talent, resulting in the EP “No Fear” and the album “Raptures”. Q: I can hardly imagine that you completely stopped making music for almost 40 years. What happened in the meantime, and how did you experience the evolution of Electronic music, both in terms of production and the way people listen to it? To what extent has all of this influenced your current collaboration and composition process? William: Well, I didn´t leave the music business. After Days Of Sorrow I played in several bands and genres living in London and then partnering a music production company in Berlin. Sure, counting back from those days Electronic music has been taking over the dance floors more and more and its variety of styles and combinations has become countless. From my point of view it has become a lot easier to produce today then it has been in the 80´s. No more studio bookings, just a DAW should do the trick today, still it´s a good thing to still know the tricks from the old days. In terms of live shows I think it has become very minimal, not musically but band wise. You see a lot of artists as a two piece on stage which is a lot easier for travel and production costs… just ask the promoters. As we still mainly perform as a four piece it has become harder to plan dates and tours. Coming back to the composition process, yes there is a different approach. There is no longer a process of hooking up with ideas in a rehearsal room, we do songwriting in our own little studio and take it from there. The one thing that hasn´t changed is that we mainly use the equipment and sounds we used in the 80´s. Q: Since your rebirth, “Raptures” is already your second album. How do you look back on the previous album, “Soulmate Sister”, and the transition or evolution toward “Raptures”? What were the main ideas, inspirations, or triggers that ultimately brought “Raptures” to life? William: “Soulmate Sister” was a good starting point for us to get going again and see what we could do as a three piece. From then on it was ideas coming from all angles getting them into our music. “Raptures” is a continuation of this whole process. It´s still the same mindset as in the early days but with a perspective of a different age, obviously both with ours and the ever-evolving world. Q: “Raptures” remains an album with strong 1980s connotations. Was this a conscious artistic choice, or is that 80s DNA simply part of who you are? And, more importantly, what kind of album did you ultimately want to create? William: It is absolutely both, its ‘Who We Are’! We wanted to strike a balance between simplicity and modern production without sounding too overwhelming. Keeping in mind that we still use the sounds of the old equipment it was the natural way to go. Q: I actually haven’t found much detailed information about “Raptures”. Is the album especially personal or intimate, or is there a deeper layer hidden within the lyrics and the title itself? Also, how did the relationship between music and lyrics develop? Did the music inspire the lyrics, or did the lyrics shape the music? William: “Raptures” is our feeling of excitement, an explosion of emotions when it comes to the music. The songs express somewhat the emotions and views on ourselves and the worldly environment, state of times, just like in the 80´s. Only this time in a more mature way including the experience of all these years, you can´t deny that you have aged. We have changed, so has the world, but our overall perspective is more or less the same. In production and writing I like to play with rhythms, sounds and melodies. Most of the times a lyric and theme idea then comes along with it.  Q: What were the key phases in the creation of this new album, and what were the biggest challenges or obstacles you had to overcome along the way? And how did you work together as a band to bring everything to fruition? William: As a matter of fact, it’s a very simple process. Two things though are very essential, time and state of mind. If you can bring those together then you are on your way to get creative and the basics laid down. In these times we are happy that I have a small studio to work in. Distance is not that big of a problem, as for instance I can send the basics over to each and everyone for input. In the end we just have to fit the ideas together. I also like to be in a studio with all of the band, but that is not really an option, logistics, expenses for studio time, etc. are not something that goes well with an underground band. Q: In the meantime, you have also returned to performing live. How have those experiences been so far, and how do you approach translating the studio production and atmosphere of the songs to the stage? William: I´m sure that everyone loves playing live… and, so do we. We´ve been doing this for four years now since our revival and its absolutely great. Making new and meeting old friends while playing your heart out, yes that´s a big, big reason for making music after all. It’s natural that on a recording part of the energy remains in the can, live is where you can release and perform of what the song and your personality is all about, and again this is really ‘Who we Are’, the first single of the album “Raptures”!

items.body: William Bleak releases the debut album “Neon Goth” in June 2026 through Breathing Records, the label’s first full-length from the Berlin-based solo project. The record mixes industrial, EBM and gothic and is out now on streaming platforms and Bandcamp. William Bleak “Neon Goth” follows the singles “Ghost Waltz” and “Black and Blue,” and the latter closes the album. “Neon Goth” began as a planned compilation of William Bleak’s 2024 singles before it became a standalone album. Bleak said the project changed after the death of a friend: “the death of a friend inspired me to create a complete piece of work – something uniquely personal.” He names Nine Inch Nails, Killing Joke and 2000s industrial metal among the album’s influences. Neon Goth by William Bleak About Breathing Records Breathing Records is an independent label based in San Diego, founded in 2025 and focused on industrial and dark electronic music. The label launched in late 2025 with the compilation “Inhale Vol. I” and also works with Matte Blvck and Unter Strøm. About William Bleak William Bleak is the solo project of a Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist, producer and songwriter. He began recording under the William Bleak name in 2016, after the end of his earlier band I Am the SVN. His early releases were rooted in surf-influenced garage rock, before the debut album “Songs of Death” moved the project toward a darker sound. After relocating to Berlin, he recorded the second album “Viva Lost Love” with a trio line-up. Bleak’s musical background combines classical music, post-punk and hardcore. His mother was an opera singer, while his father introduced him to post-punk and hardcore. He started playing guitar at age 12 after several years of piano lessons, and began producing electronic music at 15. He later DJed at different venues and parties. He plays guitar, bass, synthesizer and drums, and produces and mixes his own material. Before and alongside William Bleak, he released music under several names, including Saint Ark, Dear Envy, Weekend Dad, I am the svn and STereochan. His influences include the Japanese Visual Kei scene, with bands such as D’espairsRay, Dir en grey and MUCC, as well as experimental electronic acts including Crystal Castles, Death Grips and HEALTH. He also cites rock bands such as Death from Above 1979, The Garden and Type O Negative. His connection to gothic music dates back to childhood exposure to Killing Joke, The Cure and Siouxsie. At the same time, he has criticised parts of the gothic scene, including what he has described as “Schlager with eyeliner” when referring to certain German gothic acts. He has also questioned how gatekeepers decide what is and is not considered “goth”. In 2023, following line-up changes, Bleak rebuilt the project around a drum machine and a more electronic, aggressive sound. This phase included the singles “Crows and Ravens”, “Blood Red”, “Beat and Bleed”, “Delirium” and “Never Feel“. His lyrics draw on his frustrations with modern society, mental illness, including depression and ADHD, and a turbulent personal life. As a live act, William Bleak has shared stages with She Past Away, Clan of Xymox and Traitrs. He has also supported Ductape and Rosegarden Funeral Party, and appeared at Infest Festival in Manchester and NCN Festival in Germany. In January 2026, he signed to Breathing Records. The William Bleak project released “Neon Goth” as its debut album for the label in June 2026.

items.body: VORN release their debut album “Beyond the Sentinel” in June 2026 through Scanner, the Dark Dimensions label group, on CD and across digital and streaming platforms. This is the futurepop project of Michael Roeder, the vocalist of A Spell Inside and the former wave act Behind the Scenes, together with the Finnish poet Nicko Smith. The album follows the singles “Under the Gothic Moon” and “Faithless.” “Beyond the Sentinel” collects ten original tracks alongside additional remixes, for a total of fourteen songs. The album brings futurepop built on electronic beats, synth lines and cinematic arrangements. Beyond The Sentinel by Vorn The full tracklist is: The Grey Under the Gothic Moon (Album Version) Prophecy Against the Wind Gegen alle Zeiten A New Dawn Charon Ghost of Time Static Faithless Faithless (Extended Club Mix) Faithless (Speechless Mix) Under the Gothic Moon Guardian Angel The first single, “Under the Gothic Moon,” was released on 6 March 2026 through Scanner and was issued with an official video. The follow-up single “Faithless” also appeared with a video ahead of the album. About VORN VORN is the futurepop project of Michael Roeder, the vocalist and main writer of the German act A Spell Inside and of the earlier wave project Behind the Scenes. Roeder formed VORN with Nicko Smith, a poet from Finland. A Spell Inside has recorded for Scanner across its catalogue and returned in 2025 with the album A Spell Inside “Last”, six years after its previous record; Roeder also discussed the band’s independent approach in a Click Interview with A Spell Inside. VORN introduced the project with the single “Under the Gothic Moon” on 6 March 2026, followed by “Faithless.” With “Beyond the Sentinel,” released in June 2026 through Scanner, VORN issue their first full-length album.

items.album: This Morn’ Omina join Dark Dimensions and announce ‘Vestiges’ 30-year compilation
items.excerpt: Belgian ritual industrial act This Morn’ Omina have joined the Dark Dimensions Label Group. The announcement arrives as the project prepares to mark its 30th anniversary in 2026. To celebrate the occasion, ProNoize / Dark Dimensions will release “Vestiges – 30 Years Of Ritual Sound (1996-2026)”, a compilation collecting known, rare and previously unreleased tracks from the project’s long-running catalogue. The album will be issued as a limited edition digipak CD on 26 June 2026. About This
items.body: Belgian ritual industrial act This Morn’ Omina have joined the Dark Dimensions Label Group. The announcement arrives as the project prepares to mark its 30th anniversary in 2026. To celebrate the occasion, ProNoize / Dark Dimensions will release “Vestiges – 30 Years Of Ritual Sound (1996-2026)”, a compilation collecting known, rare and previously unreleased tracks from the project’s long-running catalogue. The album will be issued as a limited edition digipak CD on 26 June 2026. About This Morn’ Omina Formed in 1996, This Morn’ Omina have built one of the more distinctive bodies of work in ritual industrial music. The project’s sound has often moved through ceremonial percussion, hypnotic repetition, martial pressure, EBM structures, Middle Eastern tonal references and darker electronic frameworks. Rather than treating rhythm as a simple club mechanism, This Morn’ Omina use it as a form of invocation, with tracks often built around trance, pressure and transformation. Across releases such as “7 Years Of Famine”, “Le Serpent Blanc – Le Serpent Rouge” and “Les Passages Jumeaux”, the Belgian act developed a language that sits between industrial aggression and ritual intensity. The early club impact of “One-Eyed Man” helped bring the project to wider attention, but This Morn’ Omina’s identity has always reached beyond dancefloor functionality. Its work is tied to cycles, symbolic systems and a larger sense of sonic continuity. “Vestiges” is therefore positioned as more than a standard anniversary collection. The title points to traces, remains and surviving marks, which suits a project whose music has repeatedly dealt with memory, transformation and the body as a site of ritual force. The compilation revisits three decades of activity while also underlining the project’s ongoing presence within the current industrial landscape. The new signing also places This Morn’ Omina within the Dark Dimensions Label Group, whose network includes ProNoize and a wider catalogue of industrial, dark electronic and gothic releases. For a project with such a strong ritual industrial identity, the move connects past work with a new label structure as the 30-year anniversary approaches.
